# Building an interval, and what it does not say {.unnumbered} *Roughly 35 minutes. Part B is one sentence read backwards, and it is the cleverest move in the session. Part E is where most published researchers get it wrong, and you will not.* ## Part A: where do sample means fall? You have a mean and a standard error. What you want is "the true mean is around here". Getting there takes one move, and it is the reason the answer does not mean what everyone assumes. We have the wall. Where does its middle 95% sit? You pre-read the answer for a normal: about two standard deviations either side of the centre. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} quantile(many_means$sample_mean, c(0.025, 0.975)) mu + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sigma / sqrt(10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 97.5% 0.4666 0.5696 [1] 0.4674635 0.5703195 ``` ::: ::: Those agree. So **95% of sample means fall within about 1.96 standard errors of the true mean.** :::{.callout-warning} ## This is not yet a confidence interval Look at what built that: `mu` and `sigma`, the true values. It is centred on the answer. To compute it you must already know what you are trying to find out, which is useless for research and fine for teaching, because we have a teaching jar. A real confidence interval is centred on **your sample mean** and knows nothing about `mu`. The two look alike and are not the same. Keep them apart. ::: ## Part B: the flip If your sample mean lands within 1.96 SEs of the true mean 95% of the time, then 95% of the time the true mean lies within 1.96 SEs of **your sample mean**. Same statement, read backwards. "I am within a mile of the pub" and "the pub is within a mile of me" say the same thing, but the second can be computed without knowing where the pub is. That is everything. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demo_mean <- mean(demo_sample$mass_g) demo_se <- sd(demo_sample$mass_g) / sqrt(10) demo_mean + c(-1.96, 1.96) * demo_se ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5070509 0.5895491 ``` ::: ::: No `mu`, no `sigma`, only ten beans. That is a confidence interval. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Build yours, and interpret it :::: ::::{.task-container} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} student_id <- 12345678 # <- yours session_code <- 4271 # <- from the board set_my_seed(student_id, session_code) my_sample <- population |> slice_sample(n = 10) my_mean <- mean(my_sample$mass_g) my_se <- sd(my_sample$mass_g) / sqrt(10) my_ci <- my_mean + c(-1.96, 1.96) * my_se my_ci ``` ::: Then write one sentence, in your own words, saying what your interval means. Do not look anything up. Write what you actually think. You will need it in Part E. :::: ::: ## Part C: does it work? Long-run claims can be checked by running the long run. `one_interval()` lives in `R/beans.R`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} intervals <- map(1:100, \(i) one_interval(n = 10)) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(replicate = row_number(), captures_mu = lower <= mu & upper >= mu) mean(intervals$captures_mu) ggplot(intervals, aes(x = replicate, y = mean_g)) + geom_hline(yintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, colour = captures_mu, shape = captures_mu), linewidth = 0.4) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 3", name = "Captures true mean") + scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 4, `TRUE` = 16), name = "Captures true mean") + coord_flip() + labs(x = "Replicate sample", y = "Sample mean (g) with 95% CI") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.93 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![One hundred samples of ten beans, each with a 95% confidence interval. The dashed line is the true mean. Intervals that miss it are crossed.](03-confidence-intervals_files/figure-html/fig-coverage-1.png){#fig-coverage fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.callout-important} ## Read the picture properly **The dashed line never moves.** The true mean is fixed: it was fixed before the session and it is fixed now. **The intervals move**, each a different length in a different place, because each came from different beans. The randomness is not in the parameter. It is in you. ::: ## Part D: the thing that went wrong Your coverage was probably nearer 91% than 95%. That is not noise. We used 1.96, which is right only if you *know* `sigma`. You estimated it from ten beans, badly, and that makes the intervals too narrow. The fix is a wider multiplier that widens further the less data you have. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} qt(0.975, df = 9) # ten beans qt(0.975, df = 999) # a thousand ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.262157 [1] 1.962341 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} intervals_z <- map(1:1000, \(i) one_interval(n = 10, multiplier = 1.96)) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(captures_mu = lower <= mu & upper >= mu) intervals_t <- map(1:1000, \(i) one_interval(n = 10, multiplier = qt(0.975, df = 9))) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(captures_mu = lower <= mu & upper >= mu) tibble( multiplier = c("1.96 (assumes sigma known)", "2.26 (t, df = 9)"), coverage = c(mean(intervals_z$captures_mu), mean(intervals_t$captures_mu)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|multiplier | coverage| |:--------------------------|--------:| |1.96 (assumes sigma known) | 0.914| |2.26 (t, df = 9) | 0.951|
::: ::: That wider multiplier is the **t distribution**, and this is the entire reason it exists. You have derived the need for it by finding that the alternative fails. By n = 1000 the multiplier is back to essentially 1.96, which is why nobody worries about it with large samples and why you should, at n = 10. :::{.callout-tip} ## In practice You will not type `1.96` or `qt()`. R does it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(demo_sample$mass_g)$conf.int ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5006918 0.5959082 attr(,"conf.level") [1] 0.95 ``` ::: ::: Compare against your hand-built interval. Use the built-in; the point of building one by hand was never speed. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Coverage, properly (graded) :::: ::::{.task-container} 1. Change the multiplier to `qt(0.995, df = 9)` and re-run the coverage simulation. What coverage do you get? What have you built? 2. Run coverage at n = 10, 40 and 160 with the correct `t` multiplier. Does **coverage** change with n? Does interval **width**? These are different questions. :::: :::
**1.** About 99%. You have built a 99% interval, and it is wider. Higher confidence is bought with precision; you never get both. **2.** Coverage does **not** change: it holds at 95% for every n, because that is what the procedure is built to deliver. Width **does** change, falling with $\sqrt{n}$. So more data does not make you more often right, it makes you more precise while being right just as often. That is not the trade most people assume they are making. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} walk(c(10, 40, 160), \(k) { ints <- map(1:1000, \(i) one_interval(n = k, multiplier = qt(0.975, df = k - 1))) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(captures_mu = lower <= mu & upper >= mu) cat("n =", k, " coverage:", mean(ints$captures_mu), " mean width:", mean(ints$upper - ints$lower), "\n") }) ``` :::
## Part E: what the interval does not say Pick interval number 42 from your run. Does it capture the true mean? **What is the probability that it does?**
The true mean is a fixed number. Your interval, once computed, is two fixed numbers. Either the first lies between the other two or it does not. The 95% attaches to the **procedure**, not to your interval: repeat the whole business many times and 95% of the intervals you build contain the truth. Yours came from a process with a 95% hit rate, and nothing further follows about *yours*, exactly as nothing follows about one coin flip from the coin being fair. ### The six statements Hoekstra and colleagues [@hoekstra2014] gave researchers and students a 95% CI from 0.1 to 0.4 and six interpretations. Mark each before reading on. Nobody is watching. **1.** The probability the true mean is greater than 0 is at least 95%. **2.** The probability the true mean equals 0 is smaller than 5%. **3.** The null hypothesis that the true mean equals 0 is likely to be incorrect. **4.** There is a 95% probability the true mean lies between 0.1 and 0.4. **5.** We can be 95% confident the true mean lies between 0.1 and 0.4. **6.** If we repeat the experiment over and over, 95% of the time the true mean falls between 0.1 and 0.4.
Every one assigns a probability to the **parameter**, which has none: it is fixed. - **1, 2, 3** claim things about the true mean directly. Posterior statements in a frequentist coat. - **4** is the one nearly everyone endorses, and the one you probably wrote in Part B. It is a *credible* interval's statement, not a confidence interval's. - **5** hides behind "confident". Either the word means "probable", so it is statement 4, or it means nothing; do not write it. - **6** catches those who think they understand. It lets the **interval stay still** and the **true mean move**, which is backwards. The mean is nailed down; the interval varies. Look at @fig-coverage: the dashed line is the thing that does not move. The true statement, absent from the list, is about the procedure: *if we repeat the experiment, 95% of the intervals we construct will contain the true mean.*
:::{.callout-note} ## The results 120 researchers and 442 students, all in psychology, endorsed on average **more than three of the six** [@hoekstra2014]. Self-declared statistical experience did not predict performance; researchers barely beat untrained first-years. Lyu and colleagues [@lyu2020] found the same across many fields, and that respondents were **confident** while wrong. If you got several wrong you are in the ordinary condition of a working scientist. The difference is that you now know. ::: ### Why the wrong answer is so attractive Because statement 4 is what you want. You want to know about the world given your data; the interval tells you about your data given the world. Those are different conditional statements, and swapping them is a different question with a different answer. - **P(interval like mine | true mean is X)** is what you have. All of frequentist inference is this shape. - **P(true mean is X | my interval)** is what you want. It is not available here, because it is a probability about the parameter, and parameters do not have probabilities in this framework. **Which does a frequentist method give you?**
Somebody *is* allowed to say statement 4. To join them you pay an entry fee, and that fee is the next chapter. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Write it down (graded) :::: ::::{.task-container} 1. Which of the six did you endorse? Record it now; it recurs next week when the p-value invites the same error. 2. Explain to someone not on this module why "95% confident" is not "95% probable", in two sentences. :::: :::
